claims.text: ULT target is below 6 mg/dL for people on urate-lowering therapy (summary, key takeaway, targets section, table, FAQ)
claims.quote: Achieving and maintaining an SU target of <6 mg/dl over the use of no target is strongly recommended for all patients receiving ULT.

claims.text: The guideline does not set a lower target for tophaceous or more severe gout, breaking from earlier ACR and EULAR guidelines
claims.quote: Breaking from prior ACR and European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) guidelines, this guideline does not specify SU thresholds beyond <6 mg/dl for patient subsets with more severe disease (e.g., those with tophi).

claims.text: Lower levels hasten tophus resolution, but no trial data support a specific lower threshold
claims.quote: There is ample evidence that lower SU levels hasten the resolution of tophi ... there are no trial data to support lower specific thresholds for such patients.

claims.text: Treat-to-target strategy: dose titration and later dosing guided by serial urate measurements (strong recommendation); serial measurements guide dosing
claims.quote: A treat-to-target management strategy that includes ULT dose titration and subsequent dosing guided by serial SU measurements to achieve a target SU, over a fixed-dose ULT strategy, is strongly recommended for all patients receiving ULT.

claims.text: Urate checked after each dose change; start low and titrate over weeks to months, not years
claims.quote: As described above, ULT titration should occur over weeks to months, not years. ... SU concentrations should be checked after each dose titration

claims.text: Starting urate-lowering medicine at a low dose and titrating up
claims.quote: These guidelines reinforce the strategy of starting with low-dose ULT and titrating up to achieve the SU target.

claims.text: ACR defines asymptomatic hyperuricemia as serum urate 6.8 mg/dL or higher with no prior flares or tophi; 7.0 meets this cutoff
claims.quote: asymptomatic hyperuricemia, which is defined as an SU concentration of ≥6.8 mg/dl with no prior gout flares or subcutaneous tophi

claims.text: An elevated urate without gout is generally watched rather than treated
claims.quote: the benefits of ULT would not outweigh potential treatment costs or risks for the large number of patients unlikely to progress to gout

claims.text: Among people with asymptomatic hyperuricemia above 9 mg/dL, only 20 percent developed gout within 5 years
claims.quote: From observational studies, among patients with asymptomatic hyperuricemia with SU concentrations of >9 mg/dl, only 20% went on to develop gout within 5 years

claims.text: ULT strongly recommended for tophi, radiographic damage, or two or more flares a year (FAQ)
claims.quote: Initiating ULT is strongly recommended for gout patients with any of the following: ≥1 subcutaneous tophi; evidence of radiographic damage (any modality) attributable to gout; OR frequent gout flares, with frequent being defined as ≥2 annually.

claims.text: Flares treated with colchicine, NSAIDs, or glucocorticoids
claims.quote: For management of gout flares, colchicine, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, or glucocorticoids (oral, intraarticular, or intramuscular) were strongly recommended.

claims.text: Flares can occur when ULT starts; anti-inflammatory prophylaxis for 3 to 6 months recommended (figure caption)
claims.quote: Continuing concomitant antiinflammatory prophylaxis therapy for 3–6 months over <3 months, with ongoing evaluation and continued prophylaxis as needed if the patient continues to experience gout flares, is strongly recommended.

claims.text: Flare risk accompanies ULT initiation (figure: flares may rise first)
claims.quote: This strategy mitigates the risk of treatment-related adverse effects (e.g., hypersensitivity) as well as flare risk accompanying ULT initiation

claims.text: Allopurinol and febuxostat are urate-lowering drugs (table)
claims.quote: allopurinol as the preferred first-line ULT, including for those with moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease (CKD; stage >3); using a low starting dose of allopurinol (≤100 mg/day, and lower in CKD) or febuxostat (<40 mg/day)

claims.text: Weight loss: small study of 11 people, mean 5 kg loss lowered urate by mean 1.1 mg/dL; weight loss program conditionally recommended for overweight or obese gout patients
claims.quote: In a small cohort (n = 11) of obese patients, a mean weight loss of 5 kg resulted in a mean SU lowering of 1.1 mg/dl

claims.text: Weight loss program conditionally recommended for people with gout who are overweight or obese
claims.quote: Using a weight loss program (no specific program endorsed) is conditionally recommended for those patients with gout who are overweight/obese, regardless of disease activity.

claims.text: Limiting alcohol lowers urate (table)
claims.quote: SU levels among patients who limited or abstained from alcohol were 1.6 mg/dl lower compared with patients who did not do so

claims.text: Diet or individual foods have a small effect on serum urate
claims.quote: the impact of diet or individual food items on SU concentration was small

claims.text: Hydration appears as counseling for people taking uricosurics, not as a urate-lowering treatment
claims.quote: For patients who are treated with uricosurics, patients should receive counseling about adequate hydration

claims.text: Switching from hydrochlorothiazide and choosing losartan when feasible are conditionally recommended
claims.quote: Switching hydrochlorothiazide to an alternate antihypertensive when feasible is conditionally recommended for patients with gout ... Choosing losartan preferentially as an antihy-pertensive agent when feasible is conditionally recommended

claims.text: For people with a history of kidney stones, allopurinol and febuxostat lower 24-hour urinary uric acid
claims.quote: For patients with a history of urolithiasis, allopurinol and febuxostat provide benefit, as both medications lower 24-hour urinary uric acid excretion more than placebo
